artiest/the-aggrovators.text:
The Aggrovators were a Jamaican dub and reggae band in the 1970s and 1980s, and one of the most important session bands of the producer Bunny Lee. The line-up changed, because Lee used the name for whichever group of musicians he was using at the time. The name came from the record shop Lee ran in the late 1960s, Agro Sounds. Many musicians who later became famous played in it, among them Jackie Mittoo, Sly and Robbie, Tommy McCook and Aston Barrett. Carlton Santa Davis, Earl Chinna Smith, George Fully Fullwood, Ansel Collins, Tony Chin, Bobby Ellis and Vin Gordon were also regular members.

The band recorded Lee's most popular work of the 1970s. The instrumental B-sides of his singles on the Jackpot and Justice labels are usually credited to The Aggrovators, and were mixed by King Tubby. In the mid-1970s, encouraged by Lee, they helped to popularise the so-called flying cymbals sound: a fast, clipped hi-hat pattern that was prominent in roots reggae for a few years after 1974.

The Aggrovators show how important the session band was in Jamaican music: the rhythm section provided the foundation, after which producers and mixers such as King Tubby made dub versions of it.
artiest/the-aggrovators.listen: Listen to a dub track by The Aggrovators and notice the fast, clipped hi-hat pattern and how bass and drums fill the space while the mix keeps dropping parts out.

artiest/the-alan-parsons-project.text:
The Alan Parsons Project was a British rock duo, formed in London in 1975, consisting of the producer and sound engineer Alan Parsons and the singer, songwriter and pianist Eric Woolfson. Parsons had worked as an assistant on The Beatles' Abbey Road and Let It Be and had recorded Pink Floyd's The Dark Side of the Moon. He met Woolfson in the canteen of Abbey Road Studios in 1974. Woolfson wanted to manage Parsons, and came up with the idea that the music industry, like the film industry, could become a medium of the producer.

The first album, Tales of Mystery and Imagination (1976), was based on the work of Edgar Allan Poe and reached the American Top 40. According to the sleeve notes, the song The Raven was the first rock track to use a vocoder. At Arista came I Robot (1977), The Turn of a Friendly Card (1980) and Eye in the Sky (1982), eleven studio albums in all in fifteen years. Many of the albums were concept albums about science fiction, the supernatural and literary or social themes. Well-known songs include I Wouldn't Want to Be Like You, Games People Play, Time, Sirius, Eye in the Sky and Don't Answer Me. The group was more popular in North America and continental Europe than in the United Kingdom, where it never had a Top 40 single.

The sound is layered and smooth, with orchestral arrangements, synthesizers and changing singers. Thanks to Parsons's experience as an engineer, the quality of the recording comes first. The duo shows how the producer became an artist in the 1970s.
artiest/the-alan-parsons-project.listen: Listen to Sirius and notice the menacing build-up of guitar and synthesizers, growing ever faster, before the drums come in.

artiest/the-allman-brothers-band.text:
The Allman Brothers Band was an American rock band, formed in 1969 in Jacksonville, Florida. The brothers Duane and Gregg Allman founded it with Dickey Betts, Berry Oakley, Butch Trucks and Jai Johanny Johanson, known as Jaimoe. Later the group settled in Macon, Georgia. Duane played slide guitar and lead guitar, Gregg sang and played keyboards. The group had two drummers and two lead guitarists. It blended blues, jazz and country, and its live performances consisted of long improvisations and instrumental numbers.

The first two albums, The Allman Brothers Band from 1969 and Idlewild South from 1970, sold modestly. The breakthrough came with the live album At Fillmore East in 1971, with long versions of In Memory of Elizabeth Reed and Whipping Post. Duane was killed in a motorcycle accident that year and in 1972 Berry Oakley died as well. Even so the band carried on, with Eat a Peach in 1972 and Brothers and Sisters in 1973. That last album contains Ramblin' Man and Dickey Betts's instrumental Jessica. In 1995 the group was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

The Allman Brothers brought Southern rock to a large audience. They showed that a rock band could improvise like a jazz orchestra, and that guitars can complement one another instead of competing. The band stopped in 2014 after a final performance at the Beacon Theatre in New York.
artiest/the-allman-brothers-band.listen: Listen to Jessica and notice the two guitars that play the melody together and take turns. Do you hear how the piano adds a light, almost cheerful touch to it?

artiest/the-andrews-sisters.text:
The Andrews Sisters were an American close harmony vocal group from the swing and boogie-woogie era. The trio consisted of the sisters LaVerne (contralto), Maxene (soprano) and Patty (mezzo-soprano), born in Minneapolis to a Greek-Norwegian family. Patty, the lead singer, was seven when the trio began. When their father's restaurant went bankrupt, the sisters took to the road to support the family. They began as imitators of the Boswell Sisters, sang with dance orchestras and performed in vaudeville.

In 1937 they became nationally famous with Bei Mir Bist Du Schön, a Yiddish song with English lyrics by Sammy Cahn, released by Decca. Beer Barrel Polka (1939), Beat Me Daddy, Eight to the Bar (1940), Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy (1941), Don't Sit Under the Apple Tree (1942) and Rum and Coca-Cola (1945), which introduced the American public to calypso, followed. The arranger Vic Schoen and the founders of Decca, Jack and David Kapp, had a large share in the success. They were at their peak during the Second World War, and are still associated with those years. They are estimated to have sold eighty million records.

The sisters sounded tight and cheerful, with three voices singing close together over a swinging rhythm. Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy is regarded as an early example of jump blues. Later Patti Page, Bette Midler, The Pointer Sisters and Pentatonix took over their style, and in 1998 they were inducted into the Vocal Group Hall of Fame.
artiest/the-andrews-sisters.listen: Listen to Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy and notice how the three voices trade short, quick phrases above the boogie-woogie rhythm.

artiest/the-animals.text:
The Animals were an English band from Newcastle upon Tyne, formed in 1962. The original line-up consisted of the singer Eric Burdon, the organist Alan Price, the guitarist Hilton Valentine, the bassist Chas Chandler and the drummer John Steel. They played rhythm and blues and belonged to the wave of British bands that conquered America in 1964, the British Invasion.

They recorded The House of the Rising Sun in a single take on 18 May 1964 at the De Lane Lea studio in London, with the producer Mickie Most. The old folk song had been given an arrangement in a minor key in the New York folk scene, which Bob Dylan recorded in 1962. The Animals turned it into an electric pop song. Valentine plays broken chords in 6/8 time, Price a solo on a Vox Continental organ, and Burdon builds the vocal to a climax. The single lasted almost four and a half minutes, long for the time. Even so it reached number 1 in England in July 1964 and in September, in a shortened version, was number 1 in the United States for three weeks. The arrangement was credited to Price alone, which caused a row. Other hits were Don't Let Me Be Misunderstood, We Gotta Get Out of This Place and It's My Life (all 1965).

Price left in 1965 and in 1966 the original group broke up. The music journalist Dave Marsh called House of the Rising Sun the first folk rock hit. According to Steel it inspired Bob Dylan to go electric. Bruce Springsteen named the band as an influence. In 1994 The Animals were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/the-animals.listen: Listen to the opening of House of the Rising Sun: Hilton Valentine does not play the chords as a block, but note by note one after another (arpeggios), in a rocking 6/8 time. Then notice how Alan Price's organ and Eric Burdon's voice grow ever fuller and louder.

artiest/the-bad-plus.text:
The Bad Plus is an American jazz group from Minneapolis, founded in 2000 by the pianist Ethan Iverson, the bassist Reid Anderson and the drummer David King. The three had been playing together since 1989. Their first album, titled The Bad Plus, was released on Fresh Sound after they had given only three performances. A performance at the Village Vanguard brought them to the attention of Columbia Records, which signed them in 2002. The debut on Columbia, These Are the Vistas, appeared in 2003, followed by Give in 2004 and Suspicious Activity? in 2005.

Later came Prog in 2007 and For All I Care in 2008, with the singer Wendy Lewis. In 2011 they played their version of Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring. In 2017 Iverson left and Orrin Evans came in on piano. Since 2021 the group has consisted of Anderson and King with the guitarist Ben Monder and the saxophonist Chris Speed.

The trio's music combines modern, avant-garde jazz with influences from rock and pop. The group recorded covers of, among others, Nirvana, Aphex Twin, Blondie, Pink Floyd, Pixies, Rush, Black Sabbath and Bee Gees. That fits a jazz world in which musicians no longer see the music of their own youth as alien. The trio shows that an acoustic piano trio with a rock beat can sound hard without using a guitar or electronics.
artiest/the-bad-plus.listen: Listen to Smells Like Teen Spirit and first try to recognise Nirvana's song in the melody on piano. Then notice how bass and drums make the piece heavy, even without an electric guitar.

artiest/the-band.text:
The Band was a Canadian-American rock group from Toronto, with Rick Danko, Garth Hudson, Richard Manuel and Robbie Robertson, all four Canadian, and the American drummer Levon Helm. From 1958 to 1963 they were called The Hawks, the backing band of the rockabilly singer Ronnie Hawkins. In the mid-1960s they became known as Bob Dylan's first electric band, on his 1966 tour. After that they continued under the name The Band.

In 1968 the debut Music from Big Pink appeared, followed in 1969 by The Band, both received with great praise. Well-known songs include The Weight, The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down and Up on Cripple Creek. Later came Stage Fright (1970), Cahoots (1971), the live album Rock of Ages (1972), the covers album Moondog Matinee (1973) and Northern Lights, Southern Cross (1975). On 25 November 1976 the group gave a farewell concert, which Martin Scorsese released in 1978 as the film The Last Waltz. In 1983 Danko, Hudson, Helm and Manuel got back together without Robertson. After Manuel's death in 1986 and Danko's in 1999, the band stopped.

The music combines americana, folk, rock, R&B, jazz and country, with the vocals of Helm, Danko and Manuel alternating and complementing one another. Roger Waters called their debut one of the most influential records in rock history. They influenced, among others, George Harrison, Eric Clapton and the Grateful Dead.
artiest/the-band.listen: Listen to The Weight and notice how different singers take turns singing the verses and how the piano and the organ keep the song at an unhurried tempo.

artiest/the-beach-boys.text:
The Beach Boys is an American band from Hawthorne in California, founded in 1961 by the brothers Brian, Dennis and Carl Wilson, their cousin Mike Love and their friend Al Jardine. As a teenager Brian learned to pick apart the harmonies of groups such as The Four Freshmen and taught his family the backing parts. Dennis was the only real surfer and suggested singing about surfing. That is how Surfin', the first single, came about, on which, to their own surprise, the band turned out to be called The Beach Boys.

At Capitol, from 1962 one hit followed another, with songs about surfing, cars and girls: Surfin' Safari, Surfin' U.S.A. (1963), Fun, Fun, Fun and I Get Around, their first number 1. At the end of 1964 Brian stopped touring to concentrate on writing and producing. With studio musicians from Los Angeles he made ever richer arrangements, with influences from classical music and jazz. That led to Pet Sounds and the single Good Vibrations (1966). The planned album Smile was never completed, and after that Carl Wilson increasingly took over the leadership.

The Beach Boys set themselves apart from other surf bands, which mainly made instrumental music with a lot of reverb, through their five-part harmonies. Brian combined rock 'n' roll, rhythm and blues and the harmonies of older vocal groups. Pet Sounds was an inspiration to The Beatles for Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, and the band helped to get pop music taken seriously as an art form.
artiest/the-beach-boys.listen: Listen to Surfin' U.S.A. and notice the harmonies. Brian Wilson had the voices for this song double-tracked for the first time, so that they sound fuller and deeper. Hear how the backing vocals move against Mike Love's lead vocal.

artiest/the-beat.text:
The Beat was an English ska band from Birmingham, formed in 1978. The singer and guitarist Dave Wakeling, the toaster Ranking Roger, the guitarist Andy Cox, the bassist David Steele and the drummer Everett Morton were joined by Saxa, a Jamaican saxophonist who had already played with Prince Buster. The group was mixed, with Black and white members, and so belonged to the 2 Tone movement. In the United States the band was called The English Beat, to avoid confusion with an American group.

At the end of 1979 2 Tone released a ska version of Smokey Robinson's The Tears of a Clown, which reached number 6 in England. After that the band set up a label of its own, Go-Feet. Mirror in the Bathroom appeared in April 1980 and reached number 4. The song is faster and barer than ska from Jamaica, with a driving drum beat and a tight bass line. The lyrics are about vanity: people who, while shopping, mainly look at their own reflection. The debut album I Just Can't Stop It (1980), produced by Bob Sargeant, reached number 3 in England. It also contains Stand Down Margaret, an attack on Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.

After Wha'ppen? (1981) and Special Beat Service (1982) the band split up in 1983. Wakeling and Ranking Roger started General Public, while Cox and Steele formed Fine Young Cannibals with the singer Roland Gift. With The Specials and The Selecter, The Beat showed that ska, punk and soul together could form a British dance music of their own, with a political message.
artiest/the-beat.listen: In Mirror in the Bathroom, listen to the rhythm section: the drums drive the song forward at a high tempo, while the bass plays a short, repeated line. Compare the tempo with the Jamaican ska of the 1960s: here you hear the energy of punk.

artiest/the-beat-brothers.text:
The Beat Brothers was not a real band but a name on a record sleeve. It was the label for the backing group of the English guitarist and singer Tony Sheridan on his first recordings for Polydor in Hamburg. On 22, 23 and 24 June 1961 Sheridan recorded a series of songs there, under the direction of the producer Bert Kaempfert. Some were accompanied by the Beatles, some by studio musicians who remained anonymous. At that time John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Pete Best were still playing in Hamburg clubs. Stuart Sutcliffe had already left in July of that year.

The first single contained My Bonnie and The Saints and came out in Germany in October 1961. It was a small success. In 1962 an album followed called My Bonnie. Kaempfert felt that the name Beatles was too like a Hamburg dialect word with an unfortunate meaning, and so had Tony Sheridan and the Beat Brothers put on the sleeve. When the Beatles became famous, the recordings were reissued, now under their own name. Without Sheridan they also recorded Ain't She Sweet and Cry for a Shadow in the same sessions.

The name The Beat Brothers shows how much chance there was in the Beatles' beginnings. Their first recordings, well before Love Me Do, appeared under another name and on someone else's record. Today they matter mainly as a document of the Hamburg years, in which the group learned to play for hours on end.
artiest/the-beat-brothers.listen: Listen to My Bonnie by Tony Sheridan and the Beat Brothers. Notice how the Scottish folk song begins slowly and then speeds up into an ordinary rock 'n' roll number.

artiest/the-beatles.text:
The Beatles were a band from Liverpool, formed in 1960, with John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and, from August 1962, the drummer Ringo Starr. The core was older: Lennon and McCartney met on 6 July 1957 at a performance by Lennon's skiffle band The Quarrymen. Between 1963 and 1970 The Beatles released thirteen albums in England. In those years the pop record changed from a captured performance into something you build in the studio.

The band learned to play in the clubs of Hamburg, from August 1960. The debut Please Please Me was recorded in a single day on 11 February 1963 at the EMI studio on Abbey Road, with the producer George Martin. After that things moved fast. On Rubber Soul (1965) Harrison plays sitar in Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown). On Revolver (1966) tape loops and guitars played backwards can be heard. That same year the band stopped performing live, and the studio became the instrument. Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967) and Abbey Road (1969) followed. In 1970 the group broke up.

Their American success of 1964 opened the door for the British Invasion: The Dave Clark Five, The Animals and The Rolling Stones followed. Because Lennon and McCartney wrote their own songs, writing your own material became the norm, and the songwriters of the Brill Building lost ground. Harrison's sitar led to raga rock, and the studio technique of Revolver to psychedelic and progressive rock. In the 1990s Oasis again took The Beatles as its model.
artiest/the-beatles.listen: In Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds the verse is in 3/4 time and the chorus in 4/4. Listen to how the waltz turns into a straight four at the chorus, and follow the countermelody that McCartney plays on a Lowrey organ.

artiest/the-birthday-party.text:
The Birthday Party was an Australian post-punk band, active from 1977 to 1983 and first known as The Boys Next Door. The core met in the early 1970s at Caulfield Grammar School in Melbourne: the singer Nick Cave, the guitarist Mick Harvey and the drummer Phill Calvert, later joined by the bassist Tracy Pew. Under the influence of the punk explosion of 1976 they first played punk covers and later fast new wave songs of their own. In 1978 a second guitarist, Rowland S. Howard, joined, and with him the sound changed greatly.

In 1980 the group moved from Melbourne to London, where the broadcaster John Peel supported them. They released two albums, Prayers on Fire (1981) and Junkyard (1982). The 1981 single Release the Bats was influential for the emerging gothic scene. Disappointed by their time in London, their sound and performances became increasingly violent. Shortly after the move to West Berlin in 1982 the band split up. Cave, Harvey and Howard went on to build admired careers.

The music used blues, free jazz and rockabilly for gloomy, noisy soundscapes. Many songs rested on repeating bass lines and frantic, minimalist drumming, with the feedback of Howard's guitar as a trademark. Above it Cave told disturbing stories of violence and perversion. Although commercial success remained limited, the influence was great.
artiest/the-birthday-party.listen: Listen to Release the Bats and notice the tilting, sharp guitar with feedback and Cave's screaming, theatrical vocals above the racing bass line.

artiest/the-blue-diamonds.text:
The Blue Diamonds was a vocal duo of the brothers Ruud and Riem de Wolff. They were born in Batavia, present-day Jakarta, and came to the Netherlands with their parents in 1949, where the family settled in Driebergen-Rijsenburg. As teenagers they sang at school parties in bands such as The Cool Cats. The word Blue in their name referred to a colonial-era slur for Indonesians; the brothers turned it into a badge of defiance.

Their repertoire consisted mainly of songs by The Everly Brothers, and the press called them the Dutch-Indonesian Everly Brothers. Their debut single was a cover of (Till) I Kissed You. In 1960 came the breakthrough with Ramona, a song originally written for a film from 1928. Their version stayed in the Dutch charts for months, sold a million copies in Germany and even reached the American Billboard chart. Other successes from that period were Oh Carol and Little Ship. In the early 1960s they toured Indonesia with Anneke Grönloh, and in the 1980s they recorded records there in Malay.

The Blue Diamonds belonged to the generation of Indo musicians who came to the Netherlands after decolonisation and carried on the rock 'n' roll and close harmony from America there. After Ruud's death in 2000 Riem went on performing for years. In 2025 a statue of the duo was unveiled in Driebergen-Rijsenburg.
artiest/the-blue-diamonds.listen: Listen to Ramona and notice the time signature. The original song was a waltz in 3/4; The Blue Diamonds sang it in 4/4. Hear too how the two voices move together in two-part harmony, just like The Everly Brothers.

artiest/the-blue-grass-boys.text:
The Blue Grass Boys was the backing band of the American mandolinist and singer Bill Monroe, who came from Kentucky. The name refers to the nickname of his home state, the Bluegrass State. Monroe had earlier performed with his brother Charlie as The Monroe Brothers, who made recordings between 1936 and 1938. After the duo split up, Bill started a group of his own, which played at the Grand Ole Opry in the 1940s.

In that band the music took on the form that was later called bluegrass, after the name of the group. The sound combines a fast tempo, a high, piercing tenor vocal, mandolin, banjo, fiddle, guitar and double bass, and alternating solos. Many musicians who later became well known themselves played in the line-up, such as the banjo player Earl Scruggs and the guitarist Lester Flatt, who joined the group in 1945. Through the work of these musicians Scruggs's fast banjo style became a hallmark of the genre.

The Blue Grass Boys were a training ground for American roots music: anyone who played with Monroe took his way of playing to other groups. Their significance for pop history is that bluegrass, with its speed and virtuosity, became a movement of its own alongside country and folk.
artiest/the-blue-grass-boys.listen: Listen to Blue Moon of Kentucky by Bill Monroe and His Blue Grass Boys and notice the fast tempo, the high vocals and the interplay of mandolin and fiddle.

artiest/the-blue-notes.text:
The Blue Notes were a South African jazz sextet, with Chris McGregor on piano, Mongezi Feza on trumpet, Dudu Pukwana on alto saxophone, Nikele Moyake on tenor saxophone, Johnny Dyani on bass and Louis Moholo-Moholo on drums. Five of the six members came from the Eastern Cape, and the group was based in Cape Town. They became known at the National Jazz Festival of 1963 in Johannesburg. The first studio recordings for the South African Broadcasting Corporation did not appear until 2002 under the title Township Bop. They contain fairly ordinary bebop, unlike their later work.

Like Dollar Brand and Hugh Masekela, the group realised that they could only play freely by leaving the country. As a mixed band, with McGregor as the only white member, they often faced police violence. In 1964 they left. After a performance at the Antibes jazz festival they stayed in Europe, played in Zürich and Geneva and in 1965 at Ronnie Scott's in London. There they found little work, partly because British musicians saw them as intruders. According to McGregor a period in Copenhagen became a turning point. In London they played mainly at The Old Place, a laboratory of British avant-garde jazz.

The Blue Notes are regarded as one of the great free jazz groups of their time. Their music acquired a sound of its own because they absorbed African styles such as kwela into progressive jazz. In this way they had a great influence on the new generation of British jazz musicians.
artiest/the-blue-notes.listen: Listen to a recording by The Blue Notes and notice how the horns play a cheerful, African melody that becomes freer and wilder as the piece goes on.

artiest/the-bomb-squad.text:
The Bomb Squad was an American hip hop production team, best known for its work for Public Enemy. Its members included Hank Shocklee and Keith Shocklee, Eric Vietnam Sadler, Gary G-Wiz, Bill Stephney and Paul Shabazz. Chuck D of Public Enemy was also part of it, under the name Carl Ryder. Their first work was Public Enemy's debut album, Yo! Bum Rush the Show, from 1987.

The team was known for a dense, idiosyncratic production style. On a single track they often stacked dozens of samples on top of one another, and they also used harsh, atonal sounds. The result was a wall of rhythm, sirens, scratches and fragments of older records, which sounded at once wild and precisely built. For Public Enemy they made It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back in 1988 and Fear of a Black Planet in 1990, and Fight the Power for the film Do the Right Thing in 1989.

The Bomb Squad also worked for other artists, including Slick Rick, LL Cool J, Ice Cube and Bell Biv DeVoe, and made remixes for pop artists such as Peter Gabriel and Janet Jackson. Their way of sampling made it clear that a producer could be a composer working with existing recordings. The dense, messy sound they devised remained a model for hip hop producers for a long time.
artiest/the-bomb-squad.listen: Listen to Fight the Power by Public Enemy. Try to pull the layers apart: the rhythm, the repeated snatches of sound and the voices that cut in between.

artiest/the-bothy-band.text:
The Bothy Band was an Irish traditional group that existed in the mid-1970s and soon came to be regarded as one of the most influential bands in Irish folk music. The bouzouki player Dónal Lunny founded it in 1975, after leaving Planxty to start his own label, Mulligan. He brought in the piper Paddy Keenan, the flautist Matt Molloy and the fiddler Paddy Glackin. Later Mícheál Ó Domhnaill on acoustic guitar and his sister Tríona Ní Dhomhnaill on clavinet and vocals joined. The group began under the name Seachtar, Irish for seven people. The debut was on 2 February 1975 at Trinity College in Dublin.

The first album, 1975, appeared that year. It was described as a very powerful mix of driving folk-rock rhythms. Old Hag You Have Killed Me followed in 1976 and Out of the Wind Into the Sun in 1977, and in 1979 a live record, After Hours. The band played its last performance in August 1979. Afterwards the members continued to play a large part in Irish music, including in Planxty, Moving Hearts and The Chieftains.

The group played old jigs and reels with the power of a rock band, and that changed how young musicians thought about traditional music. Its influence on Irish folk music continued, long after it had stopped.
artiest/the-bothy-band.listen: Listen to the medley of The Kesh Jig, Give Us a Drink of Water, The Flower of the Flock and Famous Ballymote and notice how the melodies follow one another. Do you also hear the low bouzouki and the guitar, which as a rhythm section carry the tempo?

artiest/the-brothers-four.text:
The Brothers Four is an American folk group from Seattle, founded in 1957 by four students of the University of Washington: Bob Flick, John Paine, Mike Kirkland and Dick Foley. They belonged to the same fraternity, which explains the name. Their first performances arose from a prank by a rival fraternity, which had them phoned with an invitation to audition at the Colony Club. They were allowed to sing there anyway and were hired, for pay that consisted mainly of beer. In 1959 they moved to San Francisco and, through Mort Lewis, Dave Brubeck's manager, got a contract with Columbia.

Their second single, Greenfields (January 1960), reached number 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and sold more than a million copies. The first album The Brothers Four reached the top 20 that year. They sang The Green Leaves of Summer from the film The Alamo at the Oscar ceremony of 1961, recorded the title song of Five Weeks in a Balloon in 1962 and Hootenanny Saturday Night in 1963. The British Invasion and newer folk-rock musicians such as Bob Dylan put an end to their best period. They kept performing, particularly successfully in Japan and in American hotels. The group still exists, with a changing line-up.

The music is smooth, polished folk with four-part vocals, acoustic guitars and banjo, intended for a broad audience. The group stands for the commercial folk wave of the early 1960s, just before Dylan and folk rock set the tone.
artiest/the-brothers-four.listen: Listen to Greenfields and notice the four voices that sing the melody almost as one voice, with acoustic guitar as the only clear accompaniment.

artiest/the-buggles.text:
The Buggles was an English new wave band, formed in London in 1977. The best-known line-up was a duo: the singer and bassist Trevor Horn and the keyboard player Geoff Downes. Bruce Woolley took part briefly until 1979. Horn was then working as a producer of jingles and punk groups; Downes had played in a band and studied at the conservatoire in Leeds. They met in 1976 at an audition for Tina Charles's backing band. The name was a joke on the Beatles. Horn later said that in the punk era he deliberately wanted an ugly name.

In 1977 they recorded demos in a small room above a stonemason's in Wimbledon, including Video Killed the Radio Star. Island Records under Chris Blackwell heard the demo and offered them a contract. In September 1979 the single appeared, and reached number one in the United Kingdom and fifteen other countries. The debut album The Age of Plastic came out in January 1980, followed by singles such as Living in the Plastic Age, Clean, Clean and Elstree. The second album, Adventures in Modern Recording, followed in 1981.

Horn and Downes moved to the prog rock group Yes shortly after the first album. The Buggles ceased to exist in 1981. Their music sounds like technological pop: clear synthesizers, tight production and lyrics about the new media. On 1 August 1981 the video of Video Killed the Radio Star was the first music video on the American channel MTV. The song has since been seen as a harbinger of video clip culture, and the band later influenced acts such as Daft Punk, Justice and Phoenix.
artiest/the-buggles.listen: Listen to Video Killed the Radio Star by the Buggles. Notice the contrast between the high, almost childlike vocals and the tight synthesizer accompaniment, and what the lyrics say about radio and television.

artiest/the-bulgarian-voices-angelite.text:
The Bulgarian Voices Angelite is the name under which a Bulgarian women's choir became known in the West. The choir sings modern arrangements of traditional Bulgarian folk melodies. Almost all the singers originally come from villages, and are chosen for the beauty and openness of their voices. They follow a long training in a centuries-old singing style. That style features two-part singing, a distinctive tone colour, unusual scales, unusual time signatures and sharp harmonies.

The choir, founded in 1952 at Bulgarian radio and television, became widely known through the project Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares by the Swiss ethnomusicologist Marcel Cellier. A first record appeared in 1975. In 1986 and 1988 the label 4AD reissued two compilation albums. The label's founder Ivo Watts-Russell became fascinated by the music after receiving a cassette from Peter Murphy of Bauhaus. In 1989 Cellier received a Grammy for Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares, Volume Two.

The influence reached far. Three soloists performed as Trio Bulgarka and sang on records by Kate Bush. The Bulgarian melody Kaval sviri formed the basis of the theme music of the television series Xena: Warrior Princess. In this way the choir brought the sound of Bulgarian folk music to an audience that had never heard of Bulgaria.
artiest/the-bulgarian-voices-angelite.listen: Listen to Pilentze Pee and notice the voices, which do not blend smoothly together as in a Western choir. Do you hear the sharp harmonies between the singers and the unusual rhythms?

artiest/the-byrds.text:
The Byrds were an American rock band, formed in Los Angeles in 1964. The five original members were Roger McGuinn, Gene Clark, David Crosby, Michael Clarke and Chris Hillman. McGuinn was the only constant member in all line-ups. In early 1966 Clark left because of anxiety and the growing isolation in the group. Crosby and Clarke left at the end of 1967, after which Gram Parsons and later Clarence White joined. In 1973 the original line-up briefly reunited for the last album. In 1991 the Byrds were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

In 1965 the group made folk rock a popular genre. They combined the influence of the Beatles and other British bands with contemporary and traditional folk, on their first two albums and the hits Mr. Tambourine Man and Turn! Turn! Turn!. The sound revolved around McGuinn's jangling twelve-string Rickenbacker and the heavenly harmonies. After that they were a source for psychedelic rock and raga rock, with Eight Miles High in 1966 and the album Fifth Dimension. Younger Than Yesterday followed in 1967 and The Notorious Byrd Brothers in 1968. With Sweetheart of the Rodeo from 1968 they helped get country rock going.

Members of the group went on to build careers of their own, including in Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young and the Flying Burrito Brothers. McGuinn's guitar sound was taken up by rock music and remained influential for a long time.
artiest/the-byrds.listen: Listen to Mr. Tambourine Man by The Byrds. Notice the jangling twelve-string guitar and the harmonies that turn Bob Dylan's song into a pop song.

artiest/the-cardigans.text:
The Cardigans is a Swedish band from Jönköping. The guitarist Peter Svensson and the bassist Magnus Sveningsson, both from a heavy metal background, founded it on 31 October 1992, with the drummer Bengt Lagerberg, the guitarist Mattias Alfheim and the singer Nina Persson. Alfheim was replaced by Lars-Olof Johansson while the first album was still being recorded. The name came from Svensson, who like the others was an anglophile and was looking for something rainy, woolly and nostalgic. A demo tape won them a contract with Ola Hermanson's label.

The debut album Emmerdale appeared in 1994 in Sweden and Japan and brought the radio hit Rise & Shine. Life followed in 1995 and made the band internationally known. In 1996 First Band on the Moon appeared, with Lovefool. That song became a worldwide hit after it was used in the film Romeo + Juliet. Carnival was featured in Austin Powers in 1997. The fourth album Gran Turismo from 1998 brought, among others, My Favourite Game and Erase/Rewind. A pause followed. In 2003 they returned with Long Gone Before Daylight, a calmer album with country influences, and in 2005 Super Extra Gravity appeared.

The music of The Cardigans combines sweet, light pop melodies with sharp guitars and a sometimes bitter tone. The feel of a smooth radio pop song with just a different layer underneath became their trademark. They showed that Swedish pop could also sound guitar-driven, and that their hit fitted perfectly into film and television. After a tour in 2006 and five years of rest they got back together in 2012.
artiest/the-cardigans.listen: Listen to Lovefool by The Cardigans. Notice the contrast between the cheerful melody and the desperate lyrics, and the light, almost childlike vocals of Nina Persson.

artiest/the-cars.text:
The Cars was an American rock band, formed in Boston in 1976. The line-up consisted of Ric Ocasek (rhythm guitar), Benjamin Orr (bass), Elliot Easton (lead guitar), Greg Hawkes (keyboards) and David Robinson (drums). Ocasek and Orr shared the lead vocals. Ocasek was the leader and wrote almost every song, which later led to friction. Ocasek and Orr knew each other from Ohio, played in various bands in Columbus and Ann Arbor, and moved to Boston in the early 1970s.

In 1978 the band was named best new act in a Rolling Stone readers' poll. The debut album The Cars (1978) sold six million copies. There were four top 10 hits in the United States: Shake It Up (1981), You Might Think (1984), Drive (1984) and Tonight She Comes (1985). For You Might Think the group received the Video of the Year award at the first MTV Video Music Awards in 1984. In 1988 the band stopped. Orr died in 2000. In 2011 the last album, Move Like This, appeared, and in 2018 the group was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Ocasek died in 2019.

The Cars were at the forefront of merging guitar-driven rock of the 1970s with the new synthesizer pop of the early 1980s. The critic Robert Palmer spoke of a mixture of punk minimalism, art rock, rockabilly and the concision of power pop. The result is tight, melodic and cool, with a prominent role for the synthesizer.
artiest/the-cars.listen: Listen to Drive and notice the slow, almost sleepy synthesizer sound and the soft voice of Benjamin Orr, which gives the song a vulnerable, nocturnal atmosphere.

artiest/the-carter-family.text:
The Carter Family was an American folk group that performed and recorded between 1927 and 1956. The original line-up consisted of Sara Carter, her husband A.P. Carter and her sister-in-law Maybelle Carter, all of whom had grown up in south-western Virginia. They came from the world of mountain gospel and shape note singing, and sang tight harmonies. They made their first recordings on 1 August 1927 in Bristol, Tennessee, for the Victor Talking Machine Company, under the producer Ralph Peer. A day later Jimmie Rodgers made his first records there.

Sara sang the lead vocal and played rhythm guitar or autoharp, Maybelle sang the harmony and played lead guitar. Her style, the Carter Scratch, in which she plays melody and rhythm on the guitar at the same time, has become one of the most imitated guitar styles. Songs such as Can the Circle Be Unbroken, Wildwood Flower and Keep on the Sunny Side became standards of country music. In 1970 the group was the first to be inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame.

The Carter Family is regarded as one of the most important groups of the early twentieth century. They were the first vocal group to become country stars. Their influence reaches into bluegrass, Southern gospel, pop and rock, and into the folk revival of the 1960s. That is why their name belongs in every history of American folk music.
artiest/the-carter-family.listen: Listen to Wildwood Flower and notice the guitar. Do you hear how the melody and the accompaniment seem to come from a single instrument?

artiest/the-cats.text:
The Cats was a Dutch pop group from Volendam, formed in 1964. The band was, with a few interruptions, active until 1985 and had its most successful period from 1968 to 1975. It arose from two duos: Cees Veerman and Arnold Mühren, who began in a skiffle band, and the cousins Piet Veerman and Jaap Schilder, who modelled themselves on the Everly Brothers. Together they became The Mystic Four, later The Blue Cats, after the colour of their suits and Cees's nickname Poes (Puss). From 1966 they were called The Cats, with Theo Klouwer as drummer. They sang in English, on songs by an English songwriting duo, and sounded British.

In 1968 the group recorded Times Were When, a cover of Studio Six. Piet Veerman took over more of the lead vocals, and together with the lyrics of the bassist Arnold Mühren his sad voice made a good combination. In two years that produced five top 10 hits, including Lea, Why?, Scarlet Ribbons and Marian. The biggest success was One Way Wind, written by Mühren, which was released in 38 countries and sold more than a million copies in Germany. In 1972 Katzenspiele appeared, with their hits in German. In 1974 came the album The Love in Your Eyes, recorded in Los Angeles with session musicians.

The Cats made melodic, melancholy pop music with four-part vocals and a soft, somewhat wistful tone. As a Dutch group they were unusually successful abroad, and the band is regarded as an example of the Volendam sound.
artiest/the-cats.listen: Listen to One Way Wind and notice Piet Veerman's sad voice and the slowly rolling chorus, which sounds almost like a lullaby.

artiest/the-chemical-brothers.text:
The Chemical Brothers is an English electronic music duo, formed in 1992 in Manchester by Ed Simons and Tom Rowlands. They met in 1989 at university and shared a passion for raves and clubs. In 1992 they began DJing at a club in Manchester, at first under the name The Dust Brothers. To avoid confusion with an American production duo, they adopted the name The Chemical Brothers. Their first remixes followed in 1993 and the EP Fourteenth Century Sky came out in January 1994, with Chemical Beats.

The debut album Exit Planet Dust from 1995 refers in its title to the change of name. In 1997 Dig Your Own Hole followed, recorded in their own studio in south London. It contains Block Rockin' Beats, with a voice sample from Schoolly D and a reworked bass line by 23 Skidoo. The song won a Grammy. Surrender came in 1999, Come with Us in 2002, Push the Button in 2004 and We Are the Night in 2007. The duo worked with many guest singers, including Noel Gallagher, Beth Orton, Q-Tip and Beck.

The Chemical Brothers brought big beat, a style with heavy beats, samples and guitar-like energy, to the general public. They showed that dance music could also sound like rock. In this way they form a bridge between the rave and the pop festival.
artiest/the-chemical-brothers.listen: Listen to Block Rockin' Beats and notice the bass and the heavy drum loop that carry the whole track. Do you hear Schoolly D's voice as a rhythmic accent?

artiest/the-chi-lites.text:
The Chi-Lites is an American R&B and soul group from Chicago. The group came about in 1959 at Hyde Park Academy High School, with, among others, Eugene Record, Robert Lester, Clarence Johnson, Burt Bowen and Eddie Reed. Marshall Thompson and Creadel Jones joined later. After a few names, including Hi-Lites and Marshall and the Chi-Lites, it became simply The Chi-Lites. Eugene Record was the only songwriter and lead singer. In 1968 the group signed with Brunswick Records in Chicago, with the producer Carl Davis. Their first hit, Give It Away, reached tenth place on the Billboard R&B chart in 1969.

In 1971 and 1972 their greatest successes followed: Have You Seen Her and Oh Girl, which became number one on the Billboard Hot 100 on 27 May 1972. Both sold more than a million copies. Between 1969 and 1974 the group had eleven top 10 hits on the R&B chart and 21 on the Hot 100. They were also successful in Australia, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Canada. As the line-up changed, the work became less coherent. Jones left in 1973, and shortly afterwards Record did too.

The Chi-Lites sang smooth, melodic soul with high, vulnerable lead vocals and rich backing voices. The mood is tender and often melancholy, as in songs about lost love. In this way they belong to the Chicago soul of the early 1970s, which has since been much sampled and covered.
artiest/the-chi-lites.listen: Listen to Oh Girl and notice the soft harmonica that opens the song and Eugene Record's high, pleading lead voice.

artiest/the-chiffons.text:
The Chiffons were an American girl group from the Bronx in New York, formed in 1960. It began with three school friends from James Monroe High School: the lead singer Judy Craig, with Patricia Bennett and Barbara Lee. In 1962 Sylvia Peterson joined them at the suggestion of the songwriter Ronnie Mack. The group chose the name The Chiffons for their first single, He's So Fine, written by Mack and produced by The Tokens, known for The Lion Sleeps Tonight. The song appeared on Laurie Records and became number one in the United States, with more than a million copies sold.

The first album He's So Fine appeared shortly afterwards, followed by One Fine Day. That title song was by Gerry Goffin and Carole King. Then followed Sweet Talkin' Guy, I Have a Boyfriend, and, with Peterson as lead singer, Why Am I So Shy, Strange, Strange Feeling, The Real Thing, Up on the Bridge and My Block. Sweet Talking Guy became a top 10 hit again in 1966. In 1967 the group made its first tour of England and Germany, where in London clubs they appeared as the support act for Jimi Hendrix, with members of The Beatles and The Rolling Stones in the audience.

The sound is the girl group sound of the early 1960s: clear, playful voices, handclaps and short, catchy choruses above a brisk accompaniment. The Chiffons belong to Brill Building pop, in which writers such as Goffin and King made hits for young female singers.
artiest/the-chiffons.listen: Listen to He's So Fine and notice the repeated phrases that the backing voices sing as an echo behind the lead singer.

artiest/the-chords.text:
The Chords were a British band from south-east London, formed in 1978 when the singer and guitarist Billy Hassett and his cousin, the bassist Martin Mason, placed an advertisement in the NME. In this way they found the guitarist and songwriter Chris Pope. With the drummer Brett Ascott the group played on stage from March 1979. They soon recorded a session for John Peel on BBC Radio 1, and Paul Weller was among their early fans at one of their first concerts.

The band belonged to the mod revival of the late 1970s. Their sound linked the energy of punk with the mod of the 1960s, especially as played by The Jam and The Who. Songs such as Now It's Gone (1979) and Maybe Tomorrow (1980) reached the British charts, Maybe Tomorrow even the top 40. In 1980 the debut album So Far Away appeared, with two covers: Hold On, I'm Comin' by Sam & Dave and She Said She Said by The Beatles.

Success remained limited. At the end of 1980 Hassett was dismissed and Kip Herring, formerly singer of The Vibrators, took his place. In 1981 the group stopped. Even so The Chords remained a cult band within the mod revival. In 2010 the four original members got back together for a tour, and in 2012 performances in Australia and Japan followed. In 2019 the box set ReChordings appeared, with, among other things, unreleased material. For anyone who wants to know how the mod revival sounded outside the biggest names, this is a good way in.
artiest/the-chords.listen: Listen to Maybe Tomorrow and notice how the band combines sharp guitars with a melody that seems to come from the 1960s. Do you hear what The Jam and The Who have left behind in this sound?

artiest/the-cinematic-orchestra.text:
The Cinematic Orchestra is a British group that Jason Swinscoe founded in London in 1999. Swinscoe had studied fine art in Cardiff and worked at the London label Ninja Tune, where the group also signed. He gathered a group of jazz musicians around him, including PC (Patrick Carpenter) on turntables, the drummer Luke Flowers, the saxophonist Tom Chant and the double bassist Phil France. That same year the debut album Motion appeared.

In 2001 the Porto festival, that year European Capital of Culture, asked for new music for Man with a Movie Camera, the Soviet film by Dziga Vertov from 1929. The group played that music live at screenings of the silent film, toured with it and in 2003 released the album Man with a Movie Camera. Swinscoe reworked many of those pieces for the album Every Day (2002). Then followed Ma Fleur (2007), with the much-used To Build a Home, sung by Patrick Watson, the nature film score The Crimson Wing (2008) and To Believe (2019).

The group belongs to nu jazz and downtempo. A live band improvises together with a turntablist and electronics. In the studio Swinscoe often remixes those live recordings, so that jazz improvisation and electronic production merge and it is hard to hear where one ends and the other begins. In this way The Cinematic Orchestra uses the methods of the DJ and the producer to make jazz that sounds like film music.
artiest/the-cinematic-orchestra.listen: Listen to Man with the Movie Camera and follow how the piece is built up layer by layer and grows ever fuller. Try to hear which sounds are played live and which come from the electronics.

artiest/the-clash.text:
The Clash was formed in London in 1976. In the best-known line-up the singer and guitarist Joe Strummer, the guitarist Mick Jones, the bassist Paul Simonon and the drummer Topper Headon played; the first drummer was Terry Chimes. The Clash began in the London punk scene, alongside the Sex Pistols and The Damned. The band is important because it showed that punk did not have to be a fixed style, and because its lyrics were about politics and life in the city.

The debut The Clash (1977) already contained a cover of the reggae song Police and Thieves. On the double album London Calling, released in England in December 1979 and recorded with the producer Guy Stevens, the band mixes punk with reggae, ska, rockabilly and New Orleans rhythm and blues. The record company CBS sold it for the price of a single LP. Train in Vain, which was not listed on the sleeve, became the group's first American top 40 hit. On Pennie Smith's cover photograph Simonon smashes his bass guitar on the stage of the Palladium in New York.

The triple album Sandinista! (1980) and Combat Rock (1982), with Rock the Casbah and Should I Stay or Should I Go, followed. In January 1986 the end of the band was announced. Strummer died in 2002, and in 2003 The Clash was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Rolling Stone placed London Calling that year at number 8 on its list of the 500 greatest albums, the highest place for a punk band. The blend of punk and Jamaican music made punk an attitude rather than a sound.
artiest/the-clash.listen: London Calling (1979): notice the ending. The song fades away with a signal in Morse code spelling S-O-S, a nod to the lyrics about a city that is drowning.

artiest/the-coasters.text:
The Coasters were an American vocal group for rhythm and blues and rock and roll. They came about on 12 October 1955, when Carl Gardner and Bobby Nunn left the Los Angeles group The Robins and signed with Atlantic Records. The name refers to the move from the West Coast to the East Coast. At the end of 1957 the group got its best-known line-up: Carl Gardner, Billy Guy, Cornell Gunter and Will Dub Jones, now based in New York.

The key to their success was the collaboration with the songwriting and production duo Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller. Together they made short story songs full of humour, which often needed more takes than an ordinary song. After Down in Mexico (1956) the group broke through with Young Blood and Searchin' in 1957, a double A-side. Yakety Yak, with King Curtis on tenor saxophone, became their only number one on the pop chart and the R&B chart. Charlie Brown, Along Came Jones and Poison Ivy followed, among others.

In the 1960s hits became scarcer, partly because of changes in the line-up and changing tastes. Even so the influence remained great: their records were widely imitated and made the group an important part of the doo-wop legacy, even though they themselves did not come from doo-wop. In 1987 The Coasters were the first vocal group to be inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/the-coasters.listen: Listen to Yakety Yak and notice King Curtis's tenor saxophone and the vocals, which sound like a short scene. Do you hear how the song tells a small story, almost like a little piece of theatre?

artiest/the-comet-is-coming.text:
The Comet Is Coming was a London band that brought together jazz, electronics, funk and psychedelic rock. The three members use pseudonyms: the saxophonist Shabaka Hutchings is King Shabaka, the keyboard player Dan Leavers is Danalogue and the drummer Max Hallett is Betamax. The name comes from a piece by the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, which evokes science fiction and space. Hallett and Leavers already played together as the duo Soccer96, until Hutchings turned up on stage with his saxophone at a gig. Shortly afterwards they recorded hours of music in three days, without any material written in advance.

Their debut EP Prophecy appeared in November 2015 on The Leaf Label, the album Channel the Spirits in April 2016. That album was nominated for the 2016 Mercury Prize. In 2018 the band signed with Impulse!. Trust in the Lifeforce of the Deep Mystery (2019) received glowing reviews and mixed ambient, spoken word and influences from grime.

The band's imagery revolves around space, science fiction and B-movies. Critics called them heirs of Sun Ra, the pioneer of cosmic jazz, and saw the influence of Alice Coltrane. Hutchings explained that the crystal on the cover of Prophecy ties in with Sun Ra's idea of creating your own myths. In this way The Comet Is Coming became one of the best-known names in the new London jazz, in which improvisation and danceable electronics come together.
artiest/the-comet-is-coming.listen: Listen to a track from Channel the Spirits and notice how the saxophone, together with synthesizers and drums, creates an almost danceable cosmic atmosphere. Can you hear where the improvisation stops and the groove begins?

artiest/the-common-linnets.text:
The Common Linnets is a Dutch band, founded in 2013 by Ilse DeLange and Waylon. DeLange saw the group as a platform for Dutch artists who want to make country, Americana and bluegrass, in which the members can change. The name refers to the linnet, the songbird from which people from the east of the Netherlands, where both singers come from, derive their nickname heikneuters. The idea for the name came from the designer Rens Dekker.

The big moment came in 2014. The band represented the Netherlands at the Eurovision Song Contest in Copenhagen with Calm After the Storm, written by, among others, JB Meijers and the Americans Rob and Matthew Crosby. The song came second, behind Conchita Wurst of Austria, and gave the Netherlands its best result since the win in 1975. The debut album of the same name appeared on 9 May 2014 and reached number 1 in the Netherlands. After the Song Contest Waylon left the group for his own album. His place was taken by the American Jake Etheridge, alongside JB Meijers.

The band won the Buma Cultuur Pop Award in 2014 and an Echo Award as best international newcomer in 2015. In September 2015 the second album II followed, which again finished at the top in the Netherlands. With The Common Linnets the Netherlands brought a country and Americana sound to the big European stage, and it was a hit with audiences.
artiest/the-common-linnets.listen: Listen to Calm After the Storm and notice the harmonies of Ilse DeLange and Waylon above the acoustic guitars. Do you hear how little the song needs to stay in your head?

artiest/the-communards.text:
The Communards were a British synth-pop duo, formed in London in 1985 by the Scottish singer Jimmy Somerville and the English musician Richard Coles. Somerville had previously sung with Bronski Beat. Coles was classically trained, played mainly piano and had played the clarinet solos on Bronski Beat's hit It Ain't Necessarily So. The name refers to the revolutionaries of the Paris Commune of 1871. The bassist Dave Renwick also played with them at first.

Somerville often sang in falsetto, as a countertenor. That contrast worked especially on the duo's biggest hit, an energetic Hi-NRG version of Don't Leave Me This Way from 1986, a soul classic by Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes. The singer Sarah Jane Morris sang along with her deep voice, set against Somerville's high voice. The song spent four weeks at number one in England and became the best-selling single of 1986 in that country. Later that year So Cold the Night followed.

In 1987 the album Red came out, with, among other things, a cover of the Jackson 5's Never Can Say Goodbye and the songs Victims and For a Friend. That last song was about people with HIV and AIDS and was written in memory of the activist Mark Ashton. In 1988 the duo split up. Somerville began a solo career. Coles later became a journalist and in 2005 an Anglican priest.
artiest/the-communards.listen: Listen to Don't Leave Me This Way and notice the interplay between Jimmy Somerville's high falsetto and Sarah Jane Morris's deep voice. Do you hear how the synthesizers and the danceable rhythm transform the soul song?

artiest/the-crew-cuts.text:
The Crew Cuts, also spelled Crewcuts, were a Canadian vocal quartet from Toronto. The members, Rudi Maugeri, John Perkins, Ray Perkins and Pat Barrett, had all attended St. Michael's Choir School, the school the Four Lads also came from. In March 1952 they formed a group together, which was first called Four Tones and then Canadaires. They gave up their jobs with the Ontario government to sing full time.

Their breakthrough came in Cleveland, where the disc jockey Bill Randle gave them the name that stuck and arranged a contract with Mercury Records. In the beginning they were mainly specialists in covers of rhythm and blues songs. Their version of Sh-Boom, originally by The Chords, reached number one in the United States in 1954. Earth Angel reached number two and also did well in England and Australia. Songs of their own were successful mainly in Canada. Their covers brought rhythm and blues to a large audience.

In 1955 they played in Liverpool, where the twelve-year-old George Harrison was in the audience and the thirteen-year-old Paul McCartney got an autograph. In 1958 the group moved to RCA Records and in 1964 it stopped. In 1977 the members got back together in Nashville. In 1984, together with the Four Lads and the Diamonds, they were inducted into the Canadian Hall of Fame.
artiest/the-crew-cuts.listen: Listen to their version of Sh-Boom and notice the four voices that together carry the song. Then put the original by The Chords next to it: what is different?
